title: Traitorous Critic Fallacy
description: Responding to criticism by attacking a person's perceived favorability to an out-group or dislike to the in-group as the underlying reason for the criticism rather than addressing the criticism itself, and suggesting that they stay away from the issue and/or leave the in-group. This is usually done by saying something such as, "Well, if you don't like it, then get out!"
logical_form:
Person 1 offers criticism against group 1.

Person 2 responds to the criticism by disingenuously asking them why they don't leave group 1.

examples.example:
Gertrude: I am tired of having to fill out these forms all day. Can't we find a more efficient system?

Cindy-Lou: If you're not happy with the way we do things, we can find someone who is!
examples.explanation: Cindy-Lou did not address the concern, but essentially threatened Gertrude to shut up or lose her job. This example might also be seen as *[appeal to force](https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Appeal-to-Force)* .

examples.example:
Steve: In Sweden, college is free for citizens. How come we can't do that here?

Ed: If you like Sweden so much, move there. The USA would be glad to be rid of your liberal ass!
examples.explanation: Besides *[begging the question](https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Begging-the-Question)* (Steve did not say he liked Sweden), Ed refused to address the question asked and deflected with a disingenuous question on why Steve does not move to Sweden.

exceptions: Repeated expressions of favoritism for the out-group and dislike of the in-group could justify a why-don't-you-join-the-out-group type of response.
tips: Remember the old saying about the grass being greener on the other side.
references: This a logical fallacy frequently used on the Internet. No academic sources could be found.
